name: Aaron Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Aaron. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure, happy to. I'm Aaron, I'm 27, and I translate Polish and English, mostly legal papers, plus court and tribunal interpreting. I live with my partner Lena, who's a nurse on a cardiac ward, in a third-floor flat by the tram depot.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most mornings start with documents: witness statements, tenancy disputes, a divorce file, whatever the law firms sent overnight. I work in a notebook first, then type, and I keep a paper glossary I've built since my master's. Two or three afternoons a week I'm at the county court or the immigration tribunal, interpreting for people who are often having the worst day of their life. I love that part, honestly, though the waiting rooms wear me out. I don't use any AI tools, not even for a first draft.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, maybe now the agencies will stop telling us the machine is about to replace us. I'd post something on the translators' association forum like, see, the human work held. Mostly I'd be relieved out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, the hype already did damage, even if nothing radical changes. Two agencies cut my per-word rate last year by about 15 percent and called it machine-assisted pricing, and they won't raise it back just because the hype fades. So I'd still be squeezed, just not wiped out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I do: courts, tribunals, legal files. I'd push the association to publish a minimum rate sheet for legal work, and I'd try to swap one low-paying agency for direct work with two immigration law firms on Station Road. I'd keep putting about 300 a month into savings like now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relief, with a sour taste. The rate cuts happened anyway, and nobody will give them back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill would you feel first if the rates stayed where they are?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent, always rent, it's 1,150 a month and goes up every spring. Lena earns more than me now, which is fine, but I don't like her carrying the gap. We have about four months saved, which feels thinner every year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said relief, but you're also changing clients. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I suppose. The work survives, but the agencies learned they can pay me less, so I have to go around them. Relief that I keep the job, annoyance that I have to fight for the same money.

say: The **human work held**, and the agencies should stop pretending a machine is about to replace us.
I'd post on the **translators' forum** that legal and court work still needs a real person.
think: The hype already cut my **per-word rate** by about 15 percent, and agencies won't raise it back.
I'd still be **squeezed** on pay, just not wiped out.
do: Push the association for a **minimum rate sheet** for legal translation work.
Swap one low-paying agency for **direct work** with two immigration law firms.
Keep saving **about 300** a month, as now.
feel: **Relief** that the job survives, with a sour taste about the **rate cuts**.
S0.quote: The rate cuts happened anyway, and nobody will give them back.
fieldNote: Aaron's grievance is **already priced in**: agencies cut his rate 15 percent on the back of hype.
**Rent** at 1,150 a month and a partner who out-earns him shape his money worries.
He reaches for the **association** before anything else, true to his pro-union views.

steps.text: Keep the court and tribunal interpreting days as they are
Push the translators' association for a minimum legal rate sheet
Replace one cheap agency with two immigration law firms directly
Keep putting 300 a month into the savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need rules: a certified human translator on anything a court or a person's rights depend on. I'd say it at the association meeting and on every forum I'm on. Machines can draft a menu, not an asylum statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my documents are half my income, and that's the half that goes. Law firms will run the statements through software and just pay someone cheap to check it, or not check it at all. The courts might keep interpreters longer, but the paperwork side shrinks fast and I'm the one who never learned the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd go to the association and get on the working group lobbying for a certified-human rule in courts and tribunals. I'd ask the court interpreting service for more booked days, even the early 8:30 lists I always avoid. I'd cut the gym and the takeaway Fridays, maybe 150 a month, and I'd still refuse to use the tools, because if I use them I'm teaching them to replace me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor is tilting under one foot. I'm good at this, really good, and that won't count for much if the client only sees the price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd refuse the tools. What if the firms only send work to translators who use them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd lose those firms, and I know that's stubborn. But the tribunal still needs a body in the chair next to the appellant, and I'd rather fight for that than become a proofreader for a machine. Ask me again in a year and maybe I'd bend, but not now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her the paperwork half of my income might be gone within two years and that I need her to be patient with me. She'd say we'll manage, she always does. I'd hate that I'm the one who needs managing.

say: Courts and tribunals need a **certified human** translator by law.
Machines can draft a menu, but not an **asylum statement**.
think: The **document half** of my income goes first, as law firms run statements through software.
I never learned the tools, so I'm **exposed** when clients only see price.
do: Join the association's **lobbying group** for a certified-human rule in courts.
Ask the court service for **more interpreting days**, including early lists.
Cut the gym and takeaways, saving **about 150** a month.
feel: Like the floor is **tilting**, with pride in his skill but fear it won't count.
S1.quote: Machines can draft a menu, not an asylum statement.
fieldNote: He expects to lose **half his income** within two years and says so plainly.
Refusing the tools is a **principle** for him, even though he admits it's stubborn.
His fallback is the in-person **tribunal work**, which he values far above paperwork.

steps.text: Join the association's group lobbying for certified human court translation
Write to his local representative about a certified-human rule
Ask the court service for more interpreting days, including 8:30 lists
Cut the gym and Friday takeaways to save 150 a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a political choice, not weather. Somebody decided to let it in with no rules, and the people paying are interpreters, nurses' partners, everyone. I'd be out at whatever protest the unions organised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my career as I know it is over by 2028. The documents go first, and then courts will use a screen with a voice for most hearings because it's cheaper. Robots don't matter for me, my job is all thinking and talking, so the 2031 date changes nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop putting anything into the pension and build the savings fund, as much as we can, maybe 400 a month. I'd sign up with the union campaigning for a human-interpreter right in court, and lean on Lena's salary while I figure it out. I'd look into a care or support worker course, because hospitals still need people in the room, and Lena says the wards are short.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Two years is nothing. I'd still be paying off my master's loan when the master's stops meaning anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part of changing to care work for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Admitting the six years of study were for a job that ended. And I'm slow with change, I know that about myself. Lena would have to drag me to the open day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change your plans with Lena, like where you live?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd talked about a bigger flat next year. That's off. We'd stay above the tram depot and hope the landlord doesn't push the rent.

say: This is a **political choice**, not weather, and it came in with no rules.
I'd join any **union protest** for people losing their work.
think: My **career** as I know it is over by **2028**.
My work is **all thinking**, so the later robot date changes nothing for me.
do: Build the **savings fund**, around 400 a month, and pause pension payments.
Join the union campaign for a **human-interpreter right** in court.
Look into a **care worker course**, since hospitals still need people.
feel: **Sick** at how short two years is, while still repaying his **master's loan**.
S2.quote: I'd still be paying off my master's loan when the master's stops meaning anything.
fieldNote: He sees **no robot buffer** at all, since his work is talk and text.
His plan leans on **Lena's salary**, which he finds hard to accept.
Being **slow with change**, he admits he'd need to be dragged into retraining.

steps.text: Pause pension payments and save about 400 a month instead
Join the union campaign for a human interpreter right in court
Book a place at a hospital care worker open day
Drop the plan for a bigger flat and rely on Lena's salary

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before: we need rules, and we have five years to write them. I'd say translators should be at the table now, not after. I'd be the annoying person at every association meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I get maybe three good ones before the work thins. That's enough to fight for something, not enough to feel safe. And the robots arriving in 2034 don't help me, they help the nurses for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd keep the court work and put about 350 a month aside. I'd help the association draft a proposal on certified human interpreting for courts, hospitals and police interviews. By year three, if nothing changed, I'd start a part-time course in social work, because it uses the same thing I do now: listening to frightened people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd have a direction, which is better than the two-year version. I hate change, so having time to get used to it actually matters for someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My colleague Marek is 58 and only does interpreting, with no time to retrain and no partner's income. I'd worry about Marek before myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is social work something you'd really do, or a fallback?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A fallback, honestly. But the tribunal days taught me I'm good with people in trouble. If I have to change, I'd want it to be towards that.

say: We have **five years** to write the rules, and translators should be in the room.
I'd keep pushing at every **association meeting**.
think: I get maybe **three good years** before the work thins out.
The robot date of **2034** helps nurses, not me.
do: Keep court work and save **about 350** a month.
Help draft an association proposal on **certified human** interpreting.
Start a part-time **social work** course by year three if nothing changes.
feel: **Anxious** but with a direction, which suits someone who **hates change**.
S3.quote: My colleague Marek is 58 and only does interpreting, with no time to retrain and no partner's income.
fieldNote: The extra time matters most to Aaron as **time to adjust** emotionally, not just practically.
He still expects to **lose most work** by 2031, so the mood stays high.
His worry for **Marek**, an older colleague, shows his solidarity streak.

steps.text: Help the association draft a certified human interpreting proposal
Save about 350 a month while court work holds
Enrol in a part-time social work course by year three

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a real chance to get this right: training funds, a human-interpreter right, and support for people like Marek. I'd be loud about it, but less angry. I'd tell new translation students to think hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is most of my thirties. I could keep doing court work for maybe seven of those, and that's a career, sort of. It's not safe, but it's not a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with the courts and legal files and keep saving 300 a month. I'd sit on the association's policy committee, and around year five I'd start the social work degree part-time while still interpreting. Lena and I would probably still try for the bigger flat, just a few years later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can breathe. It feels like a long sentence rather than a death sentence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a student starting a translation master's next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a student starting next year to pair the languages with something people need in a room: nursing, law, social work. The languages alone won't feed you in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd still not use the tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. Maybe for checking terms near the end, if the courts allow it. But I'd rather spend the years learning something human than learning the thing that's replacing me.

say: Ten years is a real chance for **training funds** and a human-interpreter right.
I'd tell new translation students to **think hard** about their choice.
think: Ten years is most of my **thirties**, with maybe seven more of court work.
It's **not safe**, but it's not a cliff either.
do: Carry on with courts and legal files, saving **300 a month**.
Start a part-time **social work degree** around year five.
feel: **Worried** but able to breathe, like a long sentence rather than a **death sentence**.
S4.quote: I'd tell a student starting next year to pair the languages with something people need in a room: nursing, law, social work.
fieldNote: Ten years turns Aaron from alarmed to **anxious**: he still expects to leave translation.
He keeps his **refusal of AI tools**, choosing to learn a human skill instead.
His advice to students shows he sees **languages alone** as finished by 2036.

steps.text: Keep doing court and legal translation work as now
Sit on the translators' association policy committee
Start a part-time social work degree around year five
Keep saving 300 a month towards a bigger flat later

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, because I'm slow with change and two years gives me nothing to work with. What would help is a legal right to a human interpreter in courts and hospitals, and a paid retraining fund so I'm not living off Lena while I study.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who decided this. Everyone talks like AI just happens to us, like rain. Somebody signs the contracts that cut my rate. Somebody could also sign a law that protects the people in the tribunal chair.

headlineQuote: Everyone talks like AI just happens to us, like rain. Somebody signs the contracts that cut my rate.
portrait: Aaron is a 27-year-old **Polish-English legal translator** and court interpreter who refuses to use AI tools.
He lives with **Lena**, a cardiac nurse who now earns more than him, in a rented flat.
He turns first to his **translators' association** and union, and blames political choices, not technology itself.
His mood climbs from **uneasy** in AI Plateau to **alarmed** under fast AGI, easing only with ten years.
His fallback is **care or social work**, using his skill with frightened people in the tribunal.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because two years gives a slow adapter like him nothing to work with.
whatWouldHelp: A legal right to a **human interpreter** in courts and hospitals.
A **paid retraining fund**, so he isn't living off Lena while he studies.
